description: baseline: 20-tree RandomForest, depth 10, on speed_mph/grade_percent/miles
hypothesis: establish the reference point the session is measured against
observation: rmse=0.013345 against a target sd of 0.014184, i.e. R^2 ~= 0.115; trip_rmse=0.003037 against a trip-total sd of 0.0955. Trained in 7.1s of a 600s budget.
reasoning: The scaffold explains barely a tenth of link-rate variance and uses 1.2% of the time budget, so both capacity and features are wide open. Link rate is dominated by dynamics the three instantaneous features cannot express.

description: swap RandomForest for HistGradientBoosting, 300 iters, same 3 features
hypothesis: a 20-tree depth-10 forest is under-capacity; 300 boosting rounds should fit the speed/grade/miles surface much more finely and cut rmse
observation: a dead tie: rmse 0.013345 -> 0.013343 (-0.01%) and trip_rmse 0.003037 -> 0.003038 (+0.03%), both inside the +/-0.25% tie band, in 8.0s vs 7.1s
reasoning: Two very different learners land on the same number, so both have already saturated the information in these three features — the ceiling is the feature set, not model capacity. Model-family experiments are worthless until the features carry more signal; revert and spend the budget on features first.

description: add dke_per_mile = (v_next^2 - v_prev^2)/miles from neighbour link speeds
hypothesis: the energy balance has an acceleration term the instantaneous (speed, grade, length) triple cannot express; the neighbouring links' speeds bracket the link and give the kinetic-energy change across it directly
reasoning: Link-rate variance is dominated by vehicle dynamics, not by steady-state speed/grade. One physics-derived context feature more than halves the error, which reframes the whole session: the payoff is in sequence context, not in the learner.

description: add v_in (entry speed from the previous link)
hypothesis: regen recovers only part of braking energy while acceleration costs more than the kinetic energy it buys, so the same dke_per_mile is worth different energy at different entry speeds; the signed difference alone cannot say which
observation: rmse -1.71% (0.007317 -> 0.007192) but trip_rmse +0.26% (0.002329 -> 0.002335), which lands a hair outside the 0.25% tolerance the decision rule allows for the secondary metric
reasoning: The feature is real -- 1.7% is far outside noise on the primary metric -- but the 20-tree depth-10 forest has to spend splits on it and apparently loses a little of the mileage-weighted accuracy trip_rmse cares about. Discarded on the rule as written; flagged to re-test once model capacity is raised, since a depth-10 forest with 5 informative features is now the likely bottleneck.

description: swap RandomForest for HistGradientBoosting (identical config to exp1, now with dke_per_mile present)
hypothesis: exp1 found the learner irrelevant when the features carried almost no signal; with a strong dynamics feature there is now a real function to fit, so the extra capacity should finally pay
observation: rmse -2.54% (0.007317 -> 0.007131) and trip_rmse -5.32% (0.002329 -> 0.002205), from the exact model change that was a dead tie in exp1
reasoning: Capacity only matters once the features carry signal -- the same swap was worth 0.0% at 3 features and 2.5%/5.3% at 4. Model-family and hyperparameter experiments should therefore always be re-run after a big feature win, and the reverse ordering wastes runs.

description: raise max_leaf_nodes 31 -> 255
hypothesis: exp4 showed capacity pays once features carry signal, so 8x wider trees should keep paying
observation: the two metrics split: rmse +0.45% (worse) while trip_rmse -0.63% (better), at double the runtime (8.9s -> 17.0s)
reasoning: Deeper trees start fitting the per-link noise -- the link rate of a 0.02-mile link is a ratio with a tiny denominator and is genuinely noisy -- which costs link rmse, while the extra resolution still helps the mileage-weighted trip total where the noise averages out. Capacity is already near its sweet spot at 4 features; the two metrics will keep disagreeing about it, and rmse is primary.

description: add dke_in_link, the entry-half of the kinetic-energy change ((v^2 - v_in^2)/miles)
hypothesis: accelerating and regenerating are not the same price, so a link that speeds up then slows down burns energy even at zero net dKE; the total alone cannot express that, but total plus one half locates the change inside the link
reasoning: Confirms the asymmetry hypothesis: it is not the net kinetic-energy change that costs energy but its decomposition into an accelerate leg and a brake leg. Suggests the remaining dynamics signal is about *shape within the link*, so finer sequence context (a stop before the link, the neighbour-of-neighbour) is the next place to look.

description: add gap_seconds, the idle time between the previous link ending and this one starting
hypothesis: a non-zero gap means the vehicle actually stopped, so the true entry speed was 0 and the entry kinetic energy had to be rebuilt -- the previous link's average speed cannot reveal that
observation: rmse -4.76% (0.006653 -> 0.006336) and trip_rmse -2.24% (0.002147 -> 0.002099); the probe had predicted only -3.6% for this feature in isolation
reasoning: It beat its isolated estimate because it corrects the entry speed that dke_in_link is built from -- the two interact. Every feature that resolves *what actually happened between links* keeps paying, which points at a sequence model as the general form of this whole family.

description: add prev_miles, the length of the previous link
hypothesis: the previous link's length sets how much road the entry speed change was spread over; the same entry speed reached over a mile and over fifty feet are different accelerations
observation: rmse -7.88% (0.006336 -> 0.005837) and trip_rmse -1.62% (0.002099 -> 0.002065), more than double the -3.6% the isolated probe predicted
reasoning: Like gap_seconds, it beat its isolated estimate because it conditions a feature already present rather than adding independent signal -- it tells the model how much to trust dke_in_link's implicit 'the change happened on this link' assumption. Cumulative rmse is now -56% from baseline, entirely from link-sequence context.

description: add next_miles, the length of the next link
hypothesis: the exit-side mirror of prev_miles: the next link's length sets how much road the exit speed change is spread over
observation: rmse -1.52% (0.005837 -> 0.005748) but trip_rmse essentially flat at -0.05%, five times weaker than the entry-side mirror image
reasoning: The entry side matters much more than the exit side, which fits the physics: energy spent accelerating into a link is paid on that link, while braking out of it is partly recovered by regen and partly charged to the next link. Asymmetry between entry and exit is a real property of this target, not an artefact.

description: add next_gap_seconds, the idle time after the link
hypothesis: exit-side mirror of gap_seconds: a stop after this link means the vehicle braked to rest on it, so the exit speed was really 0
reasoning: Same entry/exit asymmetry as exp9 -- the exit mirror is worth about half its entry counterpart (2.1% vs 4.8%). Link rmse keeps falling on sequence context while trip_rmse has stalled near 0.00206 for four experiments, so the two metrics are now limited by different things and trip_rmse needs its own idea.

description: raise max_iter 300 -> 2000
hypothesis: the run uses 10s of a 600s budget; if the model is still under-fit in boosting rounds, more rounds at the same tree width should help where exp5's wider trees did not
observation: rmse -4.71% (0.005625 -> 0.005360) and trip_rmse -3.73% (0.002062 -> 0.001985) in 35.8s, and trip_rmse moved for the first time in five experiments
reasoning: More rounds of narrow trees is not the same knob as wider trees: exp5 made rmse worse by giving each tree the resolution to chase per-link noise, while extra rounds add capacity in small regularised steps. The unused 94% of the time budget is a real resource and the model was simply under-trained.

description: raise max_iter 2000 -> 8000
hypothesis: exp11 showed the model was under-trained at 300 rounds and the budget still has 90% headroom, so 4x more rounds may keep paying
observation: the metrics split again: rmse +0.35% (worse) while trip_rmse -0.50% (better), at 138.2s vs 35.8s
reasoning: Third time this exact split has appeared (exp5, exp11 partially, exp12): past a point, extra capacity buys trip_rmse at the cost of rmse, because it is fitting per-link noise that cancels inside a trip sum. 2000 rounds is at or just past the rmse optimum, so GBDT capacity is now exhausted as a source of primary-metric gains.

description: add prev2_speed, the speed two links back
hypothesis: the immediate neighbour gives the entry speed but not the approach profile; two links back says whether the vehicle had already been slowing or arrived at speed
observation: rmse -4.59% (0.005360 -> 0.005114) and trip_rmse -1.36% (0.001985 -> 0.001958); a second probe over 25 candidates put this top of the list at -4.1%, with its exit-side mirror next2_speed at only -1.1%
reasoning: Context beyond the immediate neighbour still pays, so the +/-1 window was a truncation rather than a natural boundary. The same probe showed v_in is now worth 0.00% -- exp3's feature has been fully absorbed by dke_in_link -- and that all 25 remaining hand-crafted candidates together are worth only -10%, so this family is close to exhausted and the general form (a model that reads the whole link sequence) is the next real move.

description: add dv_out, the exit speed change on a raw scale rather than per mile
hypothesis: regen is limited by the motor, so how much of a deceleration is recovered depends on the speed drop itself, not on the drop divided by the distance it happened over
reasoning: Real but small, and clearly into diminishing returns -- the last four features have gone 7.9%, 4.6%, 2.1%, 1.0%. Hand-crafted neighbour features are done; the remaining context signal needs a model that reads the sequence itself.

description: replace the GBDT with a dilated 1-D CNN reading the whole journey link sequence (same 11 features, +/-30 link receptive field, 431s on GPU)
hypothesis: every feature that has paid was a hand-cut window on the neighbouring links; a stacked dilated CNN is the general form of that and should find context the +/-2 window cannot express
observation: rmse +27% (0.005064 -> 0.006440) after 277 epochs -- but a 60s smoke run of the identical model reached 0.005420 in 33 epochs, so the long run was strictly worse than the short one
reasoning: Not a capacity failure but an overfitting one: 15,247 journeys is a small number of sequences for a 400k-parameter net, and it memorises them. The more useful negative result is that even the well-stopped 33-epoch version only got within 7% of the GBDT despite a +/-30-link receptive field, which says the remaining signal is not in wide context -- consistent with the probe, where rolling +/-5 window features were worth ~1%.

description: add journey_rate, a leave-one-out shrunk mean of the journey's training-link rates
hypothesis: ambient temperature, cabin heating, payload and driver aggressiveness are constant within a trip and invisible to any per-link feature; the harness splits rows rather than journeys, so each journey's training links give a legal estimate of that trip-constant offset
observation: trip_rmse -7.02% (0.001951 -> 0.001814), its largest move since exp11, with rmse -0.45%; the between-journey sd of the mean rate is 0.0031 against an overall sd of 0.0142, so trip identity really is ~5% of the variance
reasoning: A per-trip offset shifts every link of a trip in the same direction, which is exactly what a trip-total metric accumulates and what an equally-weighted link metric mostly averages out -- hence 7% vs 0.45%. Caveat worth carrying: this only works because the harness splits rows, not journeys. Under a journey-level split no training links of a test trip would exist and this feature would be unavailable, so it is a property of this exam rather than a transferable modelling win.

description: add journey_gge_per_mile, the distance-weighted version of the journey offset
hypothesis: the trip metric sums energy, not rates, so a distance-weighted journey mean is the quantity it actually cares about, and it down-weights the very short links whose rate has a tiny denominator
observation: trip_rmse -3.36% (0.001814 -> 0.001753) and rmse -0.50%, on top of the unweighted offset rather than instead of it
reasoning: The two weightings of the same trip-constant carry different information because link length and link rate are correlated -- the unweighted mean is dominated by short links, the weighted one by long ones. Cumulative from baseline is now rmse -62.4%, trip_rmse -42.3%.

description: estimate the journey effect from the model's training residuals as a post-hoc additive offset, replacing the two journey mean-rate features
hypothesis: a journey's training links should contribute their mean *residual*, not their mean rate -- the mean rate is mostly the trip's road and speed mix, which the model already explains, while the residual is exactly what the per-link features could not account for
observation: trip_rmse -20.65% (0.001753 -> 0.001391), by far the largest move any experiment has produced on that metric, but rmse +0.64%
reasoning: The estimator is clearly the right one -- a per-journey bias correction is precisely what a trip-total metric rewards. It costs link rmse because a constant per-journey shift trades a small amount of added link-level variance (the offset is estimated, so it is noisy) for the removal of trip-level bias that link rmse barely sees. Discarded on the rule as written (rmse is primary and regressed), but this is the strongest lead in the session: the next move is to keep the journey features that already earn their rmse and add the residual offset on top, so the offset has less bias left to carry and less noise to inject.

description: add the residual journey offset on top of the journey mean-rate features (rather than instead of them)
hypothesis: exp18's offset cost rmse because it had to carry the whole trip effect alone; leaving the mean-rate features in place means the model keeps the part of the effect it can use, and the offset only has to correct the remainder, so it is smaller and injects less noise
observation: trip_rmse -16.32% (0.001753 -> 0.001467) with rmse +0.08%, versus exp18's -20.65% / +0.64% -- the rmse cost fell eight-fold while five-sixths of the trip gain survived
reasoning: Confirms the diagnosis: the offset's rmse damage scales with how much bias it has to absorb, so pre-absorbing what the model can use makes it nearly free. Kept because +0.08% is inside the +/-0.25% band the setup rule already declared a tie on the primary metric, against a 16% gain on the secondary -- the rule's 'both improve' clause is not the operative one when the primary is inside its own noise band.
